WILLIAM

First, who this talk is for. Fintech, insurance, healthcare, telco. Here an AI agent doesn't just chat. It moves money, settles claims, reads patient records, runs part of a network.

Every sector has its own rules. Strip away the legal language, and they ask the same few questions.

Source: Ch 10 (opening lines, 10.7, 10.8) · Ch 14, 'Who is in the room'

WILLIAM

So what do we mean by verticalizing? Each of these industries has its own rulebook. A bank answers to DORA and its payment limits. An insurer's AI that prices life and health cover is high-risk under the EU AI Act, and claims need a sign-off. Healthcare has HIPAA in the US and GDPR in Europe, and patient consent. Telcos answer to NIS2 and change control.

The mistake is building a separate AI stack for each one. Verticalizing means the opposite: one platform underneath, the same identity, gateway, policy, telemetry and evals for everyone, and the domain rules expressed on top of it as policy. Change the vertical, you change the rules, not the platform.

That's what the demo shows for one vertical, insurance.

WILLIAM

Picture an auditor sitting next to you with one decision your agent made. These are the five questions they will ask. The big line is the question; the small tag is the rule behind it.

One: what did the agent do? The EU AI Act, Article 12: automatic logs, for the life of the system.
Two: who allowed it, and within what limits? FINRA calls this scope and authority.
Three: could a human stop it, or reverse it? Article 14, human oversight.
Four: can you explain this one decision to the person it affected? Article 86, and the EU court's Dun and Bradstreet ruling: "the procedure and principles actually applied". Not the model in general. Their case.
Five: are the records complete, kept, and safe from tampering? Six months at least, says Article 19. DORA wants them protected. ISO 24970, a draft standard, will say what an AI log contains.

Hold on to these five. At "From requirement to artifact" we answer them with what Northstar produces. Not legal advice.

WILLIAM

That is the stakes. For a hobby project, "the agent did something odd, so we changed the prompt" is a fine post-mortem. For a bank, an insurer, a hospital or a telco, "we don't know what the agent did" is not an answer. Not to the auditor, and not to the customer.

So let's look at an agent that wanted to move money.

Source: Ch 14, slide 09 title · Ch 10.1

WILLIAM

This is a screen from a demo insurer Kasper built, called Northstar. An AI agent handled a car-damage claim and proposed paying the customer five thousand eight hundred euros. It wasn't paid. It wasn't refused either. It is waiting.

Look at the two ringed lines. Amount: 5800. Status: awaiting approval. The agent did all the work up to the money. The platform, not the agent, decided that this one needs a person, and the agent tells the customer so.

That is the whole talk on one screen: guardrails the agent cannot move, rules that give it some autonomy, and a record of what it did and why. By the end you'll know how to build it, from upstream projects.

Notice what this screen cannot tell you: which rule held it, at what limit, who signs, and how long they take. Those are the auditor's questions two, three and four. Act 3 answers them live, and the trace answers them afterwards.

This is claim CLM-1842, from a live run of the demo.

WILLIAM

Act one. Agents don't just add more complexity. They change what kind of complexity we have. Keep moving.

Source: Ch 14

WILLIAM

You have probably seen this picture before, and that is the point.

The top row: we went from one big program, the monolith, to many small services, then to services that talk through queues, and now to agents, which pick their own next step.

The magenta row. Every step fixed a real problem, but what it broke was always the same kind of thing: we lost sight of what was going on.

The two lines at the bottom. Building got easier. Understanding got harder.

Source: Ch 1

WILLIAM

In a normal system you can draw the call graph, the map of who calls whom, on a whiteboard before it runs.

An agent is different. On the left, one prompt: "remove the free-plan accounts". Then the same prompt, run three times. Run one looks first, then deletes. Run two stops and asks a human. Run three deletes without looking. And the pink bars are the tokens each run used, so even the cost changes.

Like a taxi driver who picks a new route every ride. The code tells you what the agent may do, not what it will do. The model draws the call graph at run time. A test that passed on run two tells you nothing about run three.

Source: Ch 1

WILLIAM

We keep saying "agent", so here is the definition. An agent is a model, plus instructions, plus tools, plus a loop. The model writes the next step. The instructions are its rules. The tools are what it can touch. The loop keeps asking the model until it says "done". Watch that last part.

Source: Ch 1, 'the five terms'

WILLIAM

Here is that loop, opened up. The dashed frame is the harness, the program that runs the agent.

Follow it left to right. First, on the left: a goal comes in. The agent packs it with its instructions and its list of tools. Next: it sends that to the model, and you pay per token, in and out. Then the diamond: the model answers one of two ways. "Run this tool", and the agent runs it, often through an MCP server, adds the result and goes round again. Or "here is my final answer", and it stops.

So the model, not your code, decides when to stop. Nobody knows how many steps there will be. In a regulated domain, that is the problem.

Source: Ch 1

WILLIAM

Next come three protocols, so first: what is a protocol? An agreed way for two programs to talk, like the rules of a phone call. The agent asks "call this tool", and numbers the question, seven. The answer comes back with the same seven. MCP and A2A both work like this.

Source: Ch 2, 'In plain words' (JSON-RPC)

WILLIAM

Three open standards, one minute. Take each one by where it sits.

The lines going down first. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is how an agent gets tools it didn't ship with. Think USB-C for AI tools: build the plug once, and any agent can use it. The current spec is dated 28 July 2026, and it is stateless: no more sessions.

Then the line going across. A2A, Agent2Agent, is how agents talk to each other: a claims agent hands a case to a settlement agent. The A2A docs put it in two words: MCP is vertical, A2A is horizontal. Version 1.0 shipped on 12 March 2026, and A2A joined the Agentic AI Foundation, AAIF, on 17 August.

And the folder on the right. Skills are the simplest: a folder with a SKILL.md file and some scripts, loaded only when the task needs them. An open standard since December 2025.

None of the three is a CNCF project.

WILLIAM

If you already know observability, you don't start over. Think of this as a decoder ring. Each row: what you know, and its new shape.

A stack trace becomes a reasoning chain, and you only have it if you saved it. A status code becomes a quality signal, because a 200 OK can still carry a wrong answer. Requests per second and latency become tokens, cost and blast radius.

The last row matters most. A request you could replay becomes a run you can't repeat. So the trace you recorded is the only copy. Like a flight recorder: you can't fly the same flight twice.

And that brings us back to the auditor.

Source: Ch 1

WILLIAM

Remember the auditor's questions from the start? Here a regulator writes two of them down.

This is FINRA, which oversees US broker-dealers, in its 2026 oversight report from December 2025. It is the first US regulatory text with advice written for agents.

The first line is question two: scope and authority. Can the agent do more than it was meant to? The second line is questions one and four: can you trace it, and can you explain it? Can you show afterwards what it did, and why?

So "we don't know what the agent did" was never going to be an answer. Hold on to those two lines.

Source: Ch 10.1, 10.7 · Ch 14, slide 09

WILLIAM

Here is the whole talk in one sentence. Agents change the nature of complexity, so the platform has to decide what an agent may do, and prove it afterwards from the trace.

Three words. Decide: the platform, not the agent, says yes or no. Trace: we record what actually happened. Prove: later, someone who isn't an engineer can check it. Think of airport security: the guard decides, the camera records, and the log proves it.

None of this is new: golden paths, guardrails and observability stacks, pointed at agents. We already have the open-source pieces.

The first word needs a sharper definition. What does it mean for the platform to decide?

Source: Ch 14 · Ch 1

WILLIAM

Here is what "decide" means, and it's the line my OSFF demo was built on. You don't trust an agent to remember its own authority limits. You make the platform enforce them. An agent is a model in a loop. It can be talked into things, and it forgets. The platform doesn't.

So we draw the limits as rings, like the walls of a castle. Start in the middle.

Core, identity: who it is. Every agent gets an identity the platform can check, not a name it claims.
Ring 1, reach: what it connects to. Which other programs it can even open a connection to.
Ring 2, capability: what it may do. Which tools, and with which arguments.
And the outer ring, the keystone: it can never edit what constrains it. In an arch, the keystone is the stone that holds the others in place. If the agent could rewrite its own rules, the other three rings would mean nothing.

Hold on to these four. In Act 3 Kasper shows you each ring in Northstar, and two of them get stopped live. Kasper: how much of this does tracing already give us?
